{{Short description|Stochastic process in time series analysis}}
{{refimprove|date=December 2010}}
In the [[statistics|statistical analysis]] of [[time series]], a '''trend-stationary process''' is a [[stochastic process]] from which an underlying trend (function solely of time) can be [[Trend estimation|removed]], leaving a [[stationary process]]. The trend does not have to be linear.

Conversely, if the process requires differencing to be made stationary, then it is called [[Unit root|difference stationary]] and possesses one or more [[unit root]]s.<ref>{{cite web |title=Differencing And Unit Root Tests |url=http://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~churvich/Forecasting/Handouts/UnitRoot.pdf |website=pages.stern.nyu.edu |access-date=27 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040513093710/http://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~churvich/Forecasting/Handouts/UnitRoot.pdf |archive-date=2004-05-13 |language=en |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Burke |first1=Orlaith |title=Non-Stationary Series |url=http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~burke/Autocorrelation/Non-Stationary%20Series.pdf |website=www.stats.ox.ac.uk |publisher=[[University of Oxford]] |access-date=27 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140611005843/http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~burke/Autocorrelation/Non-Stationary%20Series.pdf |archive-date=June 11, 2014 |language=en |date=2011}}</ref> Those two concepts may sometimes be confused, but while they share many properties, they are different in many aspects. It is possible for a time series to be non-stationary, yet have no unit root and be trend-stationary. In both unit root and trend-stationary processes, the mean can be growing or decreasing over time; however, in the presence of a shock, trend-stationary processes are mean-reverting (i.e. transitory, the time series will converge again towards the growing mean, which was not affected by the shock) while unit-root processes have a permanent impact on the mean (i.e. no convergence over time).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.econ.ku.dk/metrics/Econometrics2_05_II/Slides/08_unitroottests_2pp.pdf|title=Non-Stationary Time Series and Unit Root Tests|last=Heino Bohn Nielsen|date=|website=|publisher=|access-date=}}</ref>

==Formal definition==

A process {''Y''} is said to be trend-stationary if<ref name=Nelson/> 

:<math>Y_t = f(t) + e_t,</math>

where ''t'' is time, ''f'' is any function mapping from the [[real number|reals]] to the reals, and {''e''} is a stationary process. The value <math>f(t)</math> is said to be the trend value of the process at time&nbsp;''t''.

==Simplest example: stationarity around a linear trend==

Suppose the variable ''Y'' evolves according to 

:<math>Y_t = a \cdot t + b + e_t</math>

where ''t'' is time and ''e''<sub>''t''</sub> is the error term, which is hypothesized to be [[white noise]] or more generally to have been generated by any stationary process.  Then one can use<ref name=Nelson>Nelson, Charles R. and Plosser, Charles I. (1982), "Trends and Random Walks in Macroeconomic Time Series: Some Evidence and Implications," ''[[Journal of Monetary Economics]]'', 10, 139–162.</ref><ref name=Hegwood>Hegwood, Natalie, and Papell, David H.  "Are real GDP levels trend, difference, or regime-wise trend stationary? Evidence from panel data tests incorporating structural change." http://www.uh.edu/~dpapell/realgdp.pdf </ref><ref name=Lucke>Lucke, Bernd. "Is Germany‘s GDP trend-stationary? A measurement-with-theory approach." {{cite web |url=http://www.wiso.uni-hamburg.de/fileadmin/wiso_vwl_iwk/paper/gdptrend.pdf |title=Archived copy |accessdate=2010-12-07 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110708110539/http://www.wiso.uni-hamburg.de/fileadmin/wiso_vwl_iwk/paper/gdptrend.pdf |archivedate=2011-07-08 }} </ref> [[linear regression]] to obtain an estimate <math>\hat{a}</math> of the true underlying trend slope <math>a</math> and an estimate <math>\hat{b}</math> of the underlying intercept term ''b''; if the estimate <math>\hat{a}</math> is significantly different from zero, this is sufficient to show with high confidence that the variable ''Y'' is non-stationary.  The [[errors and residuals in statistics|residuals]] from this regression are given by

:<math>\hat{e}_t = Y_t - \hat{a} \cdot t - \hat{b}.</math>

If these estimated residuals can be statistically shown to be stationary (more precisely, if one can reject the hypothesis that the true underlying errors are non-stationary), then the residuals are referred to as the '''detrended''' data,<ref name=Duke>http://www.duke.edu/~rnau/411diff.htm "Stationarity and differencing"</ref> and the original series {''Y''<sub>''t''</sub>} is said to be trend-stationary even though it is not stationary.

==Stationarity around other types of trend==

===Exponential growth trend===

Many economic time series are characterized by [[exponential growth]].  For example, suppose that one hypothesizes that [[gross domestic product]] is characterized by stationary deviations from a trend involving a constant growth rate.  Then it could be modeled as 

:<math>\text{GDP}_t = Be^{at}U_t</math>

with U<sub>t</sub> being hypothesized to be a stationary error process.  To estimate the parameters <math>a</math> and ''B'', one first takes<ref name=Duke/> the [[natural logarithm]] (ln) of both sides of this equation:

:<math> \ln (\text{GDP}_t) =  \ln B + at + \ln (U_t).</math>

This [[log-linear modeling|log-linear]] equation is in the same form as the previous linear trend equation and can be detrended in the same way, giving the estimated <math>(\ln U)_t</math> as the detrended value of <math> (\ln \text{GDP})_t  </math>, and hence the implied <math>U_t</math> as the detrended value of <math>\text{GDP}_t</math>, assuming one can reject the hypothesis that <math>(\ln U)_t</math> is non-stationary.

===Quadratic trend===

Trends do not have to be linear or log-linear. For example, a variable could have a quadratic trend:

:<math>Y_t = a \cdot t + c \cdot t^2 + b + e_t.</math>

This can be regressed linearly in the coefficients using ''t'' and ''t''<sup>2</sup> as regressors; again, if the residuals are shown to be stationary then they are the detrended values of <math>Y_t</math>.
